introduction.content: Nearly all my paintings begin on a screen and end on canvas. There is a reason for that: I belong to the last generation, the millennials, that studied without screens, with paper and pen, and then had to make its way in a digital environment. The same doubleness runs through my working life. I divide my time between the craft of art and the design and development of software, the most ethereal of the crafts.

painting.title: Painting
painting.limits: Painting is a practice as old as humanity itself. And a painter can work a surface as much as he wants; painting’s only limits are space and time. In theory those are infinite resources, but from a human point of view they are finite: the space we can take in, and the time of one life.
painting.recontextualising: Giving time and space to an image that originally had neither (a scroll is not a physical place, and the time given to an image there is minimal) changes its meaning completely. In giving it that time, that importance, you recontextualise the image, and open up the chance of finding new meanings in it. The craft itself does the same work: a casual moment fixed in oil takes on another dimension.
painting.rule: As a general rule, the larger the work and the more time given to it, the better.

images.title: Decontextualised images
images.found: For years I found them by chance on the internet, which was already a more or less infinite visual world before generative AI arrived. Between 2019 and 2023 I began using neural networks (StyleGAN, BigBiGAN) while they still “failed” considerably. That margin of error, the so-called “loss”, produced monsters no human could have come up with. My interest in painting them comes out of that fascination. Those tools have since reached a formal competence that interests me a good deal less: because they get it right too often. AI since 2023 is boring for being predictable, in the same way a predictable conversation or a predictable book is boring. The better it gets, the worse. The so-called “AI slop” floods our daily lives with images that are all alike and have no character whatsoever.
images.accident: “No mistakes, just happy accidents”, as Bob Ross used to say. What serves an artist is the accident, the singular. The software that deforms an image until it aberrates. Failure is working material.

failure.title: Failure
failure.content: “I have done many things because I have failed at all of them. I start from failure as one of the Fine Arts.” The line is from the multifaceted Pepín Tre, and it explains fairly well why I end up in such different techniques and registers. Genius and inspiration are comfortable clichés long past their sell-by date; what actually pushes you to try something else is the last thing having failed. Success, real or perceived, is paralysing. Or so I want to believe.

project.title: juanmamoreno.com, the product
project.lead: It is built on certificates of authenticity that depend on nobody but its own administrator, a catalogue anybody can browse, and a set of tools that automate the digital workflows that come of making art.

about.title: Where I am coming from
about.a: Ten years as a full-stack developer, two as a tech lead and two as a designer, over a background in artistic creation and design.
about.b: Working as a developer I was always the kind who cared more about defining and designing the solution than implementing it. Deciding what was worth building, and why, was the part that mattered to me. That is why I usually worked close to the product owners.
about.c: Now that agents have taken over almost all of the implementation and almost all of the problem-solving, moving toward product is the natural progression for me.

product.title: The product, and what it is for
product.lead: Three things, in the order they were built.

one.name: Certificates that depend on nobody
one.body: A certificate of authenticity for every physical work, written to a public chain where the artist alone holds the key. No intermediary to trust, no subscription to keep paying, and nothing that lapses if a company loses interest. The record is written into the chain itself rather than linked from it, so it survives the website, the gallery and the artist.

two.name: A catalogue anybody can read
two.body: The work — physical and generative — laid out so that anyone can move through it, narrow it, and take away what they need: the technical sheet, the certificate as a pdf, an essay about the painting, where that painting turns up elsewhere on the internet. 192 paintings written out as 400 static pages in English and Spanish, every one of them readable with no JavaScript at all.

three.name: The tooling the artist actually uses
three.body: The week-to-week work, automated end to end: correcting the photograph of a canvas, cutting it to the frame, writing and translating the text, recording the work on the chain, and posting the images and the video that were generated for it. What used to be an evening is now a few decisions and a signature.

architecture.title: How it is put together
architecture.a: The site is static in the strict sense. Every page, in both languages, is written to disk before it is published and served as files — there is no server rendering anything, which means no server to fall over, to patch, or to pay for. The build refuses to publish itself if a page came out wrong.
architecture.b: Behind it, a private containerised service does the work that cannot be static: preparing photographs, writing and translating the essays, rendering video, publishing to the social networks, and assembling the transactions. What it produces goes into a document database, and anything large into object storage.
architecture.c: The chain is Ethereum. Each certificate is a token whose content — title, medium, dimensions, year and a small photograph — is written inside the chain rather than pointed at from it, so nothing needs to stay online for the record to be readable. The web-resolution images sit in storage paid for once. The key that signs is on no server at all: every certificate is signed by hand, from a phone, which is the one thing that cannot be automated and the one thing that should not be.

rot.title: Keeping control, which is the risk in working this way
rot.a: A changelog is a record of the past and cannot become false. A requirements document is a claim about the present, and it can — quietly, and usually does.
rot.b: So every entry names the thing that proves it. A script reads the file before each deploy and refuses the build if a number is used twice, if an entry has no proof, if a proof names a file that has been deleted, or if it quotes a test that has since been renamed.
rot.c: It exists because four requirements spent fifteen releases marked “met · proven by” test specs that had been deleted several versions earlier. Nobody lied. Nobody noticed. That is the failure a requirements document is supposed to prevent and the one it is worst at preventing.
rot.d: It also reports — without failing the build — the requirements whose only proof is prose. Twenty-five of the site’s hundred and one are on that list. This page says so because the tool says so.

measured.title: Measured, not argued
measured.a: The brief for the essays was rewritten this month from evidence rather than taste. Twenty-two essays had been rewritten by hand before publishing; a hundred and thirty-six had not. Measured against each other, the edited ones ran 188 to 633 words, median 442. The untouched ones ran 613 to 874, median 748. The ranges barely overlap — and nothing else about them differed: the same sentence length, the same structure, the same argument. The brief had been asking for 650 to 900 words. It now asks for 380 to 560.
measured.b: An earlier decision was corrected the same way. A search feature re-ran on every read, so a build of 186 pages was 186 billed calls to a paid API, and a few days of building came to roughly ninety euros before anyone read the meter. The feature stopped doing that, and a check now fails any build that reaches a paid API at all — the cost cannot recur by accident.

constraint.title: Finding the real constraint
constraint.a: 157 essays written. 20 reviewed. Only a reviewed essay can be published, so everything upstream is automated and producing while everything downstream waits on one human step — and the work had been going into making the upstream faster.
constraint.b: Noticing that, and saying it out loud instead of shipping the next feature, is the job.

open.title: What is still open
open.a: The review queue that would unblock all of it is designed and not built.
open.b: 137 finished essays are unread, which means unpublished.
open.c: Twenty-five requirements have no automated proof and are listed on every build.

how.title: How this is built, plainly
how.a: Most of the code here is written by an AI agent, working to a specification I write and a review I do. That is the point rather than a footnote.
how.b: An agent will happily let a requirement rot, an abstraction spread, a cost run or a feature arrive that nobody asked for. The requirements file, the named proofs and the checks that fail a build are what make working this way safe. My part is deciding what gets built, why, in what order, and what is not worth doing — and being able to show the reasoning afterwards.

links.title: The evidence
links.note: The service behind the catalogue is in a private repository and is deliberately not linked or described here.

project.lead2: Every requirement is self-explanatory and proves for itself that it still works; the build fails when one of those proofs stops being true. That is how the project sets out to head off the greatest risk facing one implemented and deployed largely by AI agents.
